sections.b:
Of the seven letters of Ignatius, only one is to a single person: Polycarp, 'overseer of the church of the Smyrnaeans, or rather, one overseen by God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ' (Ignatius to Polycarp 1:0). Ignatius had stayed at Smyrna; Pearson and Lightfoot infer from 'I was counted worthy to see your blameless face' (Ignatius to Polycarp 1:1) that the two first met there. Eusebius: from Troas Ignatius wrote 'in particular to Polycarp', and 'knowing him very well as an apostolic man, he entrusts to him, as a true and good shepherd, the flock at Antioch' (Church History 3.36.10, the site's translation of the Greek).

The letter gives a picture of what Ignatius expected of Polycarp: patience ('Carry everyone, as the Lord carries you', Ignatius to Polycarp 1:2), firmness ('Stand firm like a struck anvil', Ignatius to Polycarp 3:1), care for widows, slaves and the married (Ignatius to Polycarp 4:1-5:2). He asked him to call a council to elect 'God's runner' for Syria and to write to the churches ahead (Ignatius to Polycarp 7:2-8:1). Polycarp's own letter shows that he expected to send an envoy to Syria, and that he sent Ignatius's letters on to Philippi (Polycarp to the Philippians 13:1-2).

common: Ignatius to Polycarp is the only one of Ignatius's seven letters addressed to one person.
uncommon: The later Antiochene account of Ignatius's martyrdom made Polycarp his fellow-student under John; Lightfoot thinks Ignatius to Polycarp 1:1 shows they had not met before Smyrna.

sections.b: Written from Troas as Ignatius's guards prepared to sail suddenly for Neapolis (Ignatius to Polycarp 8:1). Ignatius gives Polycarp short rules for a church leader, turns to the Smyrnaean church as God's soldiers with Latin army words (Ignatius to Polycarp 6:2), and hands him the task of organizing envoys to Antioch (Ignatius to Polycarp 7:2-8:1).
sections.refs: Ignatius to Polycarp 1:2-3; Ignatius to Polycarp 6:1-2; Ignatius to Polycarp 7:1-8:1

sections.b: Ignatius tells Polycarp to have wives 'be content with their husbands, in flesh and in spirit' and husbands 'love their wives as the Lord loves the church' (Ignatius to Polycarp 5:1, after Ephesians 5:25-29). Then: 'Men and women who marry should make their union with the overseer's approval, so that the marriage may follow the Lord and not desire' (Ignatius to Polycarp 5:2). The verse asks for the overseer's approval; it does not describe a ceremony. Lightfoot connects it with Paul's 'only in the Lord' (1 Corinthians 7:39).

'If anyone is able to remain in purity for the honor of the Lord's flesh, let him remain so without boasting. Should he boast, he is lost; and if it becomes known beyond the overseer, he is ruined' (Ignatius to Polycarp 5:2). Lightfoot: the person's purpose is shared with the overseer but not paraded, which 'contrasts with the usage of a later age', and there is 'no indication here of an "order" of virgins'. The Catholic Encyclopedia (1910) cites the chapter for virginity 'made the subject of a vow'.

Ignatius tells Polycarp not to look down on male and female slaves, and says the slaves should not be puffed up, but serve for God's glory to gain 'a better freedom' from God, and should not 'long to be set free from the common fund, so that they are not found to be slaves of desire' (Ignatius to Polycarp 4:3). Lightfoot reads it as assuming a church fund that could be used to free slaves, and explains the warning by the fund's limits. It does not forbid freedom; on the two readings of Paul's 'make use of it', see 1 Corinthians 7:21.

sections.h: The overseer as the widows' guardian
sections.b: 'The widows must not be neglected. After the Lord, you must be the one who cares for them' (Ignatius to Polycarp 4:1). The overseer takes on personally the care that Acts 6 gave to the Seven and 1 Timothy 5 sets out in detail.

'Let your baptism remain as your weapons, your faith as a helmet, your love as a spear, your endurance as full armor' (Ignatius to Polycarp 6:2). Lightfoot: the passage 'was doubtless suggested by Ephes. vi. 13-17', though the pieces are assigned differently; 'full armor' is Paul's panoplia. Ignatius adds the soldier's pay, desertion, and the 'deposits' and 'back pay' of the Roman army's savings.

Ignatius calls Polycarp 'a perfect athlete' (Ignatius to Polycarp 1:3) and 'God's athlete', whose 'prize' (thema, a money-prize of the games, Lake) is 'incorruption and eternal life' (Ignatius to Polycarp 2:3); 'A great athlete takes the blows and wins' (Ignatius to Polycarp 3:1). Lake: 'athlete' was 'a favourite name for Christians who strove to excel in virtue, especially in ascetic practices'.
sections.refs: Ignatius to Polycarp 1:3; Ignatius to Polycarp 2:3; Ignatius to Polycarp 3:1; 1 Corinthians 9:24-27

sections.h: The one above time, visible for our sake
sections.b: 'Wait for the one who is above time: the timeless, the invisible, visible for our sake; the untouchable, beyond suffering, able to suffer for our sake; who endured in every way for our sake' (Ignatius to Polycarp 3:2). The pair 'beyond suffering' and 'able to suffer' is that of Ignatius to the Ephesians 7:2.
sections.refs: Ignatius to Polycarp 3:2; Ignatius to the Ephesians 7:2; John 1:14; 1 John 1:1

sections.b: Ignatius asks Polycarp to call a council and elect someone 'who can be called God's runner' to go to Syria (Ignatius to Polycarp 7:2), and to have the churches ahead send messengers or letters too (Ignatius to Polycarp 8:1).
sections.refs: Ignatius to Polycarp 7:1-8:1; Polycarp to the Philippians 13:1

sections.b: Ignatius's letter to Smyrna's overseer shows the church's widows, slaves, married and single members (Ignatius to Polycarp 4-5), and greets by name 'the wife of the procurator', Attalus and Alce (Ignatius to Polycarp 8:2-3). Lightfoot notes that the name Attalus 'appears many times in inscriptions and coins belonging to Smyrna'.
sections.refs: Ignatius to Polycarp 4:1-5:2; Ignatius to Polycarp 8:2-3; Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 13:2
